Seed-based functional connectivity asks a simple question: which target
regions co-vary with a chosen seed region once nuisance signals are removed?
This page starts from a spatial `neuroim` object, extracts named ROIs, and then
builds the analysis from the same pieces used for a GLM: a dataset that owns
its timing, a nuisance model, the `residualize` projection, and `fmri_lm`
itself.

The input is already preprocessed. Motion correction, registration, spatial
normalization, and denoising decisions happen upstream. This tutorial begins
at the point where an aligned four-dimensional image and its regions of
interest are ready for modeling.

## Define and extract the spatial ROIs

The synthetic image below has a non-identity signed affine and 160 time
points. The seed drives two target regions at different strengths; a control
region shares only a nuisance signal. `cuboid_roi` defines each region on the
image grid. `series_roi` returns an `ROIExtractionResult`, not an anonymous
array.

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import neuroim as ni

import fmrimod as fm
from fmrimod import baseline_model, design_matrix
from fmrimod.residualize import residualize
from fmrimod.spec import covariate
from fmrimod.stats import seed_target_correlation, seed_target_lm

rng = np.random.default_rng(13)
n_time = 160
spatial_shape = (7, 6, 5)
affine = np.array(
    [
        [-2.0, 0.0, 0.0, 10.0],
        [0.0, 2.0, 0.0, -6.0],
        [0.0, 0.0, 2.5, -5.0],
        [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0],
    ]
)
space_3d = ni.NeuroSpace.from_affine(affine, spatial_shape)
space_4d = ni.NeuroSpace.from_affine(
    affine, spatial_shape + (n_time,)
)
reference = ni.DenseNeuroVol(np.ones(spatial_shape), space_3d)

rois = {
    "seed": ni.cuboid_roi(
        reference, centroid=[1, 2, 2], surround=[0, 1, 1], fill=1
    ),
    "strong": ni.cuboid_roi(
        reference, centroid=[3, 2, 2], surround=[0, 1, 1], fill=1
    ),
    "moderate": ni.cuboid_roi(
        reference, centroid=[5, 2, 2], surround=[0, 1, 1], fill=1
    ),
    "control": ni.cuboid_roi(
        reference, centroid=[3, 5, 2], surround=[0, 0, 1], fill=1
    ),
}

motion = rng.normal(size=(n_time, 6))
seed_signal = rng.normal(size=n_time)
data = rng.normal(scale=0.6, size=spatial_shape + (n_time,))
for name, coupling in {
    "seed": 1.0,
    "strong": 0.65,
    "moderate": 0.35,
    "control": 0.0,
}.items():
    coords = rois[name].coords
    data[tuple(coords.T)] += coupling * seed_signal + 0.4 * motion[:, 0]

image = ni.DenseNeuroVec(data, space_4d)
roi_results = {
    name: image.series_roi(roi)
    for name, roi in rois.items()
}
```

The extraction receipts make the boundary inspectable. Each result records
the source-space hash, ROI mask hash, method, dimensions, and coordinates.
The assertions verify that every extraction still points to the source
affine and time axis.

```{python}
assert all(result.n_timepoints == n_time for result in roi_results.values())
assert all(
    np.allclose(result.space.affine, affine)
    for result in roi_results.values()
)

pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {
            "ROI": name,
            "result": type(result).__name__,
            "time x voxels": str(result.values.shape),
            "method": result.provenance.method_name,
            "space receipt": result.provenance.source_affine_hash,
            "mask receipt": result.mask_hash,
        }
        for name, result in roi_results.items()
    ]
)
```

## Build a dataset from pre-extracted ROI signals

Connectivity operates on one representative series per ROI. We average the
voxel series within each extraction result and keep the ROI names in a
DataFrame. Only here, after spatial extraction and its receipts are visible,
do those named series cross into fmrimod's matrix-backed dataset seam. This is
pre-extracted ROI data, not flattened voxel data.

```{python}
roi_frame = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        name: result.values.mean(axis=1)
        for name, result in roi_results.items()
    }
)
target_names = list(roi_frame.columns[1:])

dataset = fm.fmri_dataset(roi_frame.to_numpy(), tr=2.0)
pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "runs": [dataset.n_runs],
        "time points": [dataset.n_timepoints],
        "ROI columns": [str(tuple(roi_frame.columns))],
    }
)
```

## Declare the nuisance model

The drift, intercept, and motion confounds are a `baseline_model`, not a
hand-assembled nuisance matrix. The model owns its column structure.

```{python}
bmodel = baseline_model(
    basis="poly",
    degree=2,
    sframe=dataset.sampling_frame,
    intercept="runwise",
    nuisance_list=[motion],
)

design_matrix(bmodel).shape   # (time, drift + intercept + motion columns)
```

## Residualize through the model

`residualize` dispatches on the model. Pass `bmodel` itself, not its
matrix. This is the same projection the first-level seam uses, so the cleaned
signal is consistent with how fmrimod fits everything else.

```{python}
clean = residualize(bmodel, dataset.get_all_data())
clean.shape
```

## Seed-to-Target Correlation

For a cleaned ROI matrix, the effect-size estimate is one explicit call. The
helper preserves the readable "seed versus target columns" shape and adds
Fisher-*z* columns for group-ready effect sizes.

```{python}
seed_target_correlation(
    clean,
    seed=0,
    target_names=target_names,
).round(3)
```

## Seed as a GLM Covariate

The fmrireg-style inferential version treats the seed time series as a sampled
BOLD covariate. In fmrimod that is not a separate connectivity language:
`covariate(...)` is an identity-HRF term, so it enters the same `fmri_lm`
path as an ordinary authored model term.

```{python}
seed_source = pd.DataFrame({"seed": clean[:, 0]})
target_events = pd.DataFrame({
    "onset": [0.0],
    "duration": [0.0],
    "trial_type": ["seed"],
    "run": [1],
})
target_dataset = fm.fmri_dataset(clean[:, 1:2], tr=2.0, events=target_events)

seed_fit = fm.fmri_lm(covariate("seed", source=seed_source), target_dataset)
seed_index = seed_fit.design_columns().names.index("seed")
round(float(seed_fit.coef()[seed_index, 0]), 3)
```

For the common many-target ROI table, `seed_target_lm` is the compact helper on
that same idea: it fits each target on `[intercept, confounds, seed]` and
reports the seed coefficient, standard error, *t*, and *p*.

```{python}
seed_target_lm(
    dataset.get_all_data(),
    seed=0,
    confounds=design_matrix(bmodel),
    add_intercept=False,
    target_names=target_names,
).to_frame().round(3)
```

## Back to fmrimod for Group-Ready Effect Sizes

`seed_target_correlation` already includes the Fisher *z* and sampling variance
`1 / (n - 3)`, which is exactly what the group seam (`fmri_meta`, `group_fit`)
expects per connection. The lower-level `r_to_z` helper remains available when
you already have correlations from another source.

```{python}
fc = seed_target_correlation(clean, seed=0)
z = fc["fisher_z"].to_numpy()
z_var = fc["z_variance"].to_numpy()
pooled_r = fm.z_to_r(z.mean())

pd.DataFrame({
    "fisher_z": z,
    "z_variance": z_var,
}).round(3)
```

```{python}
round(float(z.mean()), 3), round(float(pooled_r), 3)
```

The `strong` and `moderate` targets carry the planted correlations, while the
`control` target stays near zero after nuisance removal. Fisher *z* and its
variance are now in the form the group-level tools expect, so a connectivity
result can flow into the same second-level analysis as any other effect.
